chapter.name: Magnetism and Matter
chapter.blurb: The chapter treats magnetism as a subject in its own right: the bar magnet and its field lines, the bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid with dipole far fields obtained by analogy with the electric dipole, and the torque and potential energy of a magnetic dipole in a uniform field. It then states Gauss's law for magnetism, which expresses the absence of magnetic monopoles. Finally it defines magnetisation, magnetic intensity, susceptibility and permeability and uses them to classify materials as diamagnetic, paramagnetic or ferromagnetic.

scope_in.item: Recall the commonly known ideas about magnets: the earth as a magnet, naming of north and south poles of a freely suspended magnet, repulsion of like and attraction of unlike poles, impossibility of isolating a pole, magnets made from iron and its alloys

Interpret the iron-filings pattern of a bar magnet as that of a magnetic dipole and state and use the four properties of magnetic field lines (closed loops, tangent gives direction of B, density gives magnitude, no intersection); plot lines with a compass needle; explain why they are not lines of force
Reason about cutting a magnet, identifying a magnetised bar using two bars only, and whether every configuration (e.g. a toroid) has poles (Example 5.1)

Explain the bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid (Ampere's hypothesis, similar field lines and compass deflections, cutting a solenoid) and use the far axial field B = (mu0/4 pi)(2m/r^3); compute the magnetic moment m = N I A of a solenoid

Use the electrostatic analogue (E to B, p to m, 1/(4 pi epsilon0) to mu0/(4 pi)) and Table 5.1 to write and compute the equatorial field -(mu0/4 pi)(m/r^3) and axial field (mu0/4 pi)(2m/r^3) of a short bar magnet, with directions

Calculate the torque m B sin(theta) and potential energy -m B cos(theta) of a dipole in a uniform field, with zero of energy at 90 degrees; identify stable (theta = 0) and unstable (theta = 180 degrees) equilibrium; find work done in turning a magnet; state that the net force is zero in a uniform field

Explain why an iron nail near a magnet experiences a net attractive force (induced moment in a non-uniform field), and analyse equilibrium and potential energy of one needle in the field of another (Examples 5.1(b), 5.2)

Define magnetic flux through an area element, state Gauss's law for magnetism, contrast it with Gauss's law of electrostatics, relate it to the non-existence of monopoles, and state how it would change if monopoles existed

Judge whether given field-line patterns can be magnetic or electrostatic (lines from a point or plate, crossing lines, closed loops round empty space, toroid, solenoid ends, bar magnet, pole pieces) and answer the conceptual points of Example 5.4
Define magnetisation M = m_net/V and magnetic intensity H = B/mu0 - M with their units; use B = B0 + Bm, Bm = mu0 M, B = mu0 (H + M), H = n I in a solenoid
Use M = chi H, mu_r = 1 + chi, mu = mu0 mu_r and B = mu H to compute H, M, B and the magnetising current for a solenoid with a core (Example 5.5); state which quantities are dimensionless
Classify materials as diamagnetic, paramagnetic or ferromagnetic from chi, mu_r and mu (Table 5.2) and from their motion in a non-uniform field and the behaviour of field lines

Describe the atomic picture and give the book's examples for diamagnetism (including superconductors and the Meissner effect), paramagnetism (thermal disorder, temperature dependence, saturation) and ferromagnetism (domains, hard and soft ferromagnets, permanent magnets, change to paramagnet at high temperature)

concepts.name: The bar magnet, its poles and magnetic field lines
concepts.description: The commonly known properties of magnets and their poles, the bar magnet as a magnetic dipole, and the properties of magnetic field lines.
concepts.idea: A bar magnet is a magnetic dipole whose two poles can never be separated, and its field is pictured by field lines that form continuous closed loops.
concepts.rule: The earth behaves as a magnet whose field points approximately from the geographic south to the geographic north, so a freely suspended bar magnet settles north-south; the tip pointing to geographic north is called its north pole and the other its south pole. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. The poles cannot be isolated: a bar magnet cut transverse to its length or along its length gives two magnets, each with a north and a south pole, so isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist. Iron filings around a short bar magnet form a pattern that suggests the magnet is a magnetic dipole, and a similar pattern is seen around a current-carrying solenoid. Magnetic field lines (i) form continuous closed loops, unlike the lines of an electric dipole which begin on the positive charge and end on the negative charge; (ii) have a tangent at each point that gives the direction of the net field B there; (iii) are more crowded per unit area where B is larger; (iv) never intersect, because the field direction at a crossing would not be unique. They can be plotted by placing a small compass needle at many positions. They are not lines of force: they do not give the direction of the force on a moving charge. The field of a bar magnet is strongest at its two ends and weakest at its central region, which lets one tell a magnet from an unmagnetised iron bar using the two bars alone. Not every magnetic configuration has poles: a toroid and a straight infinite conductor have no net magnetic moment and no poles.
concepts.example: A bar magnet cut transverse to its length, or along its length, gives two magnets, each with a north and a south pole; no piece with a single pole can ever be obtained.

questions.q: When a bar magnet is freely suspended, the tip that points towards the geographic north is called its
questions.a: north pole

questions.q: When the north poles of two magnets are brought close together, the force between them is one of ____ (write one word: attraction or repulsion).
questions.a: repulsion

questions.q: The magnetic field lines of a bar magnet
questions.a: form continuous closed loops
o: begin on the north pole and end on the south pole
begin on the south pole and end on the north pole
spread out from each pole and never return

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the commonly known ideas about magnets listed at the start of the chapter on magnetism and matter?
questions.a: A bar magnet broken into two halves gives one piece with only a north pole and one piece with only a south pole
o: A bar magnet broken into two halves gives one piece with only a north pole and one piece with only a south pole
Like poles of two magnets repel and unlike poles attract
A freely suspended bar magnet points in the north-south direction
Magnets can be made out of iron and its alloys

questions.q: Why can two magnetic field lines never intersect?
questions.a: Because the magnetic field would not have a unique direction at the point of intersection
o: Because the magnetic field would not have a unique direction at the point of intersection
Because the magnetic field is always zero where two lines meet
Because field lines carry like charges that repel one another
Because every field line is a perfect circle of the same radius

questions.q: In a map of magnetic field lines, far more lines cross unit area near point X than near point Y. What does this show?
questions.a: The magnitude of B is larger at X than at Y
o: The magnitude of B is larger at X than at Y
The magnitude of B is larger at Y than at X
B has the same magnitude at X and at Y
B points in opposite directions at X and Y

questions.q: The pattern of iron filings sprinkled around a short bar magnet suggests that the magnet behaves like
questions.a: a magnetic dipole, with two poles like the two charges of an electric dipole
o: a magnetic dipole, with two poles like the two charges of an electric dipole
a source with no poles at all

questions.q: Why does a freely suspended bar magnet come to rest along the north-south direction?
questions.a: Because the earth itself behaves as a magnet, with its field pointing approximately from geographic south to geographic north
o: Because the earth itself behaves as a magnet, with its field pointing approximately from geographic south to geographic north
Because gravity pulls unequally on the two poles of the magnet
Because the rotation of the earth drags the magnet into line
Because electric charges on the surface of the earth attract the two poles

questions.q: A pattern of iron filings similar to that around a bar magnet is observed around which of these?
questions.a: A current-carrying solenoid

questions.q: P is a point on a curved magnetic field line. The direction of the net magnetic field B at P is along
questions.a: the tangent to the field line at P
o: the tangent to the field line at P
the normal to the field line at P
the straight line joining P to the nearest pole
the straight line joining P to the centre of the magnet

questions.q: The north pole of magnet X is brought near one end of a freely suspended magnet Y, and that end of Y swings away from X. That end of Y is
questions.a: a north pole
o: impossible to identify from this observation

questions.q: Two identical-looking iron bars A and B are tested by bringing their ends together in every possible combination. Every combination shows attraction and none shows repulsion. What can be concluded about the two bars, and why?
questions.a: Only one of the two bars is magnetised. If both were magnets, some combination would bring like poles together and they would repel; attraction in every case means a magnet is simply attracting an unmagnetised iron bar.
s: Conclusion - only one bar is magnetised
Reason - two magnets would repel in some position (like poles); always attractive means one is plain iron

questions.q: Must every magnetic field configuration have a north pole and a south pole? Answer with reference to the field of a toroid.
questions.a: Not necessarily. Poles appear only if the source of the field has a net non-zero magnetic moment. A toroid (like a straight infinite conductor) has no net magnetic moment, so its field has no north or south pole.
s: Not necessarily - only when the source has a net non-zero magnetic moment
Toroid has no net magnetic moment, hence no poles

questions.q: A diagram shows the magnetic field lines of a current-carrying solenoid as perfectly straight lines that stay confined at both ends and outside, never curving. The diagram is
questions.a: wrong, because the lines must curve out at both ends and eventually meet to form closed loops
o: wrong, because the lines must curve out at both ends and eventually meet to form closed loops
right, because the field of a solenoid is uniform everywhere
right, because magnetic field lines never bend
wrong, because a solenoid has no magnetic field outside or at its ends

questions.q: A student draws the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet as lines that start on the north pole and stop on the south pole, with nothing drawn inside the magnet. Explain what is wrong with this picture, describe the correct picture, and state how it differs from the field lines of an electric dipole.
questions.a: Magnetic field lines do not start or stop anywhere: they form continuous closed loops. The lines that leave one end of the magnet and enter the other end continue through the inside of the magnet, so each line closes on itself, just as the lines of a solenoid emerge from one face and enter the other. For an electric dipole the lines really do begin on the positive charge and end on the negative charge (or escape to infinity), so they are not closed loops.
s: Magnetic field lines form continuous closed loops - they do not start or stop on poles
Correct picture - lines continue through the inside of the magnet to close each loop
Contrast - electric dipole lines begin on the positive and end on the negative charge

questions.q: Assertion (A): The magnetic field lines of a bar magnet form continuous closed loops. Reason (R): Isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) are not known to exist, so there is no point at which a magnetic field line can begin or end. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: In a field-line map of a bar magnet, point X lies just outside one end of the magnet and point Y lies beside the middle of the magnet. Compare the strength of the magnetic field at X and Y and say how the map shows it.
questions.a: The field is stronger at X than at Y, because the field of a bar magnet is strongest at its two ends (poles) and weakest at its central region. On the map this appears as field lines crowded closely (many per unit area) near X and spread out near Y.
s: Field stronger at X (end/pole) than at Y (central region)
Shown by more field lines crossing per unit area near X

questions.q: Two identical-looking iron bars A and B are given, and exactly one of them is magnetised. Using nothing but the two bars, work out a procedure to find which one is the magnet and explain the reasoning behind it.
questions.a: Use the fact that a bar magnet is strongest at its ends and weakest at its central region. Pick up A and lower one of its ends first onto an end of B and then onto the middle of B. If A feels a pull at the end of B but no force at the middle of B, then B is the magnet (its middle is the weak region). If the pull is the same at the end and at the middle of B, then A is the magnet, since the strong end of A attracts plain iron anywhere.
s: Principle - a bar magnet is strongest at its ends and weakest at its middle
Procedure - touch an end of A to an end of B and then to the middle of B
Inference - no force at the middle of B means B is the magnet; no change means A is the magnet

questions.q: Some textbooks call magnetic field lines 'magnetic lines of force'. Evaluate whether this name is appropriate.
questions.a: It is not appropriate. Magnetic field lines give the direction of the field B (the direction a small magnetised needle aligns), not the direction of the force on a moving charge; the magnetic force on a moving charge is always normal to B. Calling them lines of force is therefore misleading.
s: Judgement - the name is misleading / not appropriate
Reason - the lines show the direction of B, while the force on a moving charge is normal to B

questions.q: Design an activity to map the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet and to show, from your map, where the field is strongest.
questions.a: Place the magnet under a sheet of paper or glass. Either sprinkle iron filings and tap the sheet, or place a small compass needle at many positions and mark the direction in which it settles. Join the marked directions into smooth curves so that the needle direction is the tangent at each point; these are the field lines. The regions where the lines (or filings) are most crowded, which are the two ends of the magnet, are where the field is strongest.
s: Method - iron filings or a small compass needle placed at many positions around the magnet
Drawing - join the needle directions into curves whose tangent gives the field direction
Reading - the most crowded lines (near the ends) mark the strongest field

concepts.name: Bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid: far field and the electrostatic analogue
concepts.description: Treating a bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid, its far axial and equatorial fields, and obtaining these from electric dipole results by the dipole analogy.
concepts.idea: A bar magnet behaves like a solenoid of circulating currents, and far away its field is that of a dipole of magnetic moment m, found from the electric dipole formulas by replacing p with m and 1/(4 pi epsilon0) with mu0/(4 pi).
concepts.rule: A current loop acts as a magnetic dipole, and Ampere's hypothesis says all magnetic phenomena can be explained by circulating currents. Because the field lines of a bar magnet and of a current-carrying finite solenoid look alike, and a compass needle is deflected similarly near both, a bar magnet can be thought of as a large number of circulating currents, like a solenoid. Cutting a bar magnet in half is like cutting a solenoid: two smaller solenoids with weaker magnetic properties result, with field lines still continuous, emerging from one face and entering the other. The far axial field of a finite solenoid is B = (mu0/4 pi)(2m/r^3), which is also the far axial field of a bar magnet, so the magnetic moment of a bar magnet equals that of the equivalent solenoid producing the same field. A solenoid of N turns, area A and current I has magnetic moment m = N I A (from the previous chapter). By the electrostatic analogue, replace E by B, p by m and 1/(4 pi epsilon0) by mu0/(4 pi): for r much larger than the size l of the magnet the equatorial field is B_E = -(mu0/4 pi)(m/r^3), opposite in direction to m, and the axial field is B_A = (mu0/4 pi)(2m/r^3), along m. The same analogy gives torque m x B and energy -m.B in an external field.
concepts.example: A short bar magnet of moment 0.48 A m^2 gives, at 10 cm, 0.96 x 10^-4 T on its axis and 0.48 x 10^-4 T on its equatorial line.

questions.q: A bar magnet of size l has magnetic moment m. At a point on its axis at distance r from its centre, with r much greater than l, the magnitude of its magnetic field is
At a far point on the equatorial line (normal bisector) of a short bar magnet, the direction of its magnetic field is
questions.a: opposite to the direction of the magnetic moment m
o: opposite to the direction of the magnetic moment m
the same as the direction of the magnetic moment m
perpendicular to the magnetic moment m
undefined, because the field there is zero

questions.q: The hypothesis that all magnetic phenomena can be explained in terms of circulating currents is named after the scientist ____ (write the surname only).
questions.a: Ampere

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the replacements used in the chapter to turn the electric dipole field into the far field of a bar magnet?
questions.a: r^3 is replaced by r^2
o: 1/(4 pi epsilon0) is replaced by mu0/(4 pi)

questions.q: Why may a bar magnet be thought of as an equivalent solenoid?
questions.a: Because its field lines resemble those of a solenoid, suggesting it is like a large number of circulating currents
o: Because its field lines resemble those of a solenoid, suggesting it is like a large number of circulating currents
Because a bar magnet contains a hidden battery that drives a current along its length
Because a bar magnet has free electric charges collected at its two ends
Because the magnetic field is zero inside both a bar magnet and a solenoid

questions.q: For a short bar magnet, what is the ratio of the magnitude of the field at a far point on the axis to that at a point on the equatorial line at the same distance?
When the distance of a far axial point from a short bar magnet is doubled, the magnetic field there falls to 1/n of its earlier value. The whole number n is ____.
Explain how the idea that a bar magnet is equivalent to a solenoid is made firm, and what this says about the magnetic moment of a bar magnet.
questions.a: The axial field of a finite solenoid is calculated, and at large distances it has the same form as the far axial field of a bar magnet found experimentally. So a bar magnet and a solenoid produce similar fields, and the magnetic moment of a bar magnet is equal to the magnetic moment of the equivalent solenoid that produces the same magnetic field.
s: Far axial field of a finite solenoid has the same form as the far axial field of a bar magnet
So the magnet's moment equals the moment of the equivalent solenoid giving the same field

questions.q: In the solenoid picture, cutting a bar magnet in half is like cutting a solenoid in half. What results?
questions.a: Two smaller solenoids, each with weaker magnetic properties
o: Two smaller solenoids, each with weaker magnetic properties
Two pieces, one acting as an isolated north pole and the other as an isolated south pole
Two pieces that have no magnetic properties at all
Two solenoids, each stronger than the original

questions.q: A short bar magnet has magnetic moment 0.40 A m^2. Take mu0/(4 pi) = 10^-7 T m/A. What is the magnitude of its magnetic field at a point on its axis 0.20 m from its centre?
A closely wound solenoid has 500 turns, each of area 2.0 x 10^-4 m^2, and carries a current of 2.0 A. What is its magnetic moment?

A short bar magnet has a magnetic moment of 0.60 A m^2. Take mu0/(4 pi) = 10^-7 T m/A. Find the magnitude and direction of its magnetic field at a distance of 10 cm from its centre on (a) the axis and (b) the equatorial line.
questions.a: r = 10 cm = 0.10 m, so r^3 = 1.0 x 10^-3 m^3. (a) Axis: B = (mu0/4 pi)(2m/r^3) = 10^-7 x 2 x 0.60 / (1.0 x 10^-3) = 1.2 x 10^-4 T, along the direction of the magnetic moment (from the south pole to the north pole). (b) Equatorial line: B = (mu0/4 pi)(m/r^3) = 10^-7 x 0.60 / (1.0 x 10^-3) = 6.0 x 10^-5 T, opposite to the direction of the magnetic moment.
s: Correct formulas with r = 0.10 m
Axis - 1.2 x 10^-4 T along the magnetic moment
Equatorial line - 6.0 x 10^-5 T opposite to the magnetic moment

questions.q: A closely wound solenoid of 1000 turns and area of cross-section 2.0 x 10^-4 m^2 carries a current of 5.0 A. Its magnetic moment, in A m^2 and as a whole number, is ____.

At a far point on the equatorial line of a short bar magnet, at distance r from its centre, the field has magnitude 3.0 x 10^-5 T. What is the magnitude of the field at a point on the axis at distance 2r from the centre?

A closely wound solenoid of 800 turns and area of cross-section 2.5 x 10^-4 m^2 carries a current of 5.0 A. Take mu0/(4 pi) = 10^-7 T m/A. Treating it as a bar magnet, find its magnetic moment and the magnitude and direction of its field at a far point on its axis 0.50 m from its centre.
questions.a: Magnetic moment m = N I A = 800 x 5.0 x 2.5 x 10^-4 = 1.0 A m^2, directed along the axis of the solenoid. Far axial field B = (mu0/4 pi)(2m/r^3) with r^3 = (0.50)^3 = 0.125 m^3, so B = 10^-7 x 2 x 1.0 / 0.125 = 1.6 x 10^-6 T, directed along the axis in the direction of the magnetic moment.
s: m = N I A = 1.0 A m^2
B = 1.6 x 10^-6 T along the axis, in the direction of m

questions.q: Consider these statements about a bar magnet and a current-carrying finite solenoid. (I) When a current-carrying solenoid is cut in half, the field lines of each half are still continuous, emerging from one face and entering the other. (II) At large distances the field lines of a bar magnet and of a finite current-carrying solenoid look completely different from each other. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: The far-field formulas for a bar magnet hold for r much greater than l, the size of the magnet. A student uses the axial formula at a point 1 cm beyond the end of a 10 cm long bar magnet. Analyse whether the result can be trusted.
questions.a: It cannot be trusted. The formula treats the magnet as a short dipole and is valid only when the distance r from the centre is much greater than the size of the magnet. Here the point is about 6 cm from the centre, which is smaller than the 10 cm length, so the condition r much greater than l fails and the simple 1/r^3 dipole form does not describe the field.
s: Formula valid only for r much greater than the size l of the magnet
Here r is comparable to or smaller than l, so the result is unreliable

questions.q: A short bar magnet has magnetic moment m. Point A is on its axis at distance d from its centre and point B is on its equatorial line at distance 2d from its centre, both far from the magnet. Compare the magnitudes and the directions of the fields at A and B.
questions.a: At A: B_A = (mu0/4 pi)(2m/d^3), along m. At B: B_B = (mu0/4 pi)(m/(2d)^3) = (mu0/4 pi)(m/(8 d^3)), opposite to m. Ratio B_A : B_B = 2 : (1/8) = 16 : 1. So the field at A is 16 times that at B, and the two fields point in opposite directions (anti-parallel).
s: B_A = (mu0/4 pi)(2m/d^3), along m
B_B = (mu0/4 pi)(m/(8 d^3)), opposite to m
Ratio 16 : 1, and the fields are anti-parallel

questions.q: A student says: 'A bar magnet has no wire and no battery, so it is wrong to treat it as a solenoid.' Evaluate this objection.
questions.a: The objection is not sound. The equivalence does not need a visible wire: the field lines of a bar magnet and a solenoid are alike, a compass needle is deflected similarly near both, and the far axial field has the same form. By Ampere's hypothesis the magnet can be thought of as a large number of circulating currents, so it has the same magnetic moment as an equivalent solenoid.
s: Judgement - the objection is not valid
Reason - similar field lines/compass deflections and same far axial field; magnet as many circulating currents

questions.q: For a short electric dipole of moment p, the field at distance r is -p/(4 pi epsilon0 r^3) on the equatorial line and 2p/(4 pi epsilon0 r^3) on the axis. State the rule of replacement given by the electrostatic analogue and use it to construct the corresponding two results for a short bar magnet of magnetic moment m.
questions.a: Rule: replace E by B, p by m and 1/(4 pi epsilon0) by mu0/(4 pi) (that is, 1/epsilon0 by mu0). Equatorial field of the bar magnet: B_E = -(mu0/4 pi)(m/r^3), opposite to m. Axial field of the bar magnet: B_A = (mu0/4 pi)(2m/r^3), along m. Both hold for r much greater than the size of the magnet.
s: Replacement rule - E to B, p to m, 1/(4 pi epsilon0) to mu0/(4 pi)
Equatorial field -(mu0/4 pi)(m/r^3)
Axial field (mu0/4 pi)(2m/r^3)

concepts.name: Magnetic dipole in a uniform magnetic field: torque, potential energy and equilibrium
concepts.description: The torque and potential energy of a magnetic needle or bar magnet in a uniform field, stable and unstable equilibrium, and the work done in turning it.
concepts.idea: In a uniform field a magnetic dipole feels no net force but a restoring torque m x B, and has potential energy -m.B, lowest when m is parallel to B.
concepts.rule: A needle of magnetic moment m in a uniform field B experiences a torque tau = m x B, of magnitude m B sin(theta), where theta is the angle between m and B; it is a restoring torque that tends to align m with B. The net force on the dipole in a uniform field is zero. The magnetic potential energy is U = -m B cos(theta) = -m.B, with the zero of potential energy chosen at theta = 90 degrees (needle perpendicular to the field). U is minimum (-mB) at theta = 0, the most stable position, and maximum (+mB) at theta = 180 degrees, the most unstable position. The work needed from an external torque to turn the dipole equals the change in potential energy. In a non-uniform field, such as that of a bar magnet acting on an iron nail, the nail acquires an induced magnetic moment and experiences a net force as well as a torque; the force is attractive because the induced unlike pole is nearer the magnet than the induced like pole. For two needles, the potential energy is that of one needle in the field of the other: equilibrium is stable when its moment is parallel to that field and unstable when anti-parallel.
concepts.example: A magnet of moment 1.5 J/T aligned with a 0.22 T field needs 0.33 J of work to be turned normal to the field and 0.66 J to be turned opposite to it.

questions.q: A magnetic needle of magnetic moment m makes an angle theta with a uniform magnetic field B. The magnitude of the torque on it is
questions.a: m B sin(theta)

questions.q: With the zero of potential energy chosen when the needle is perpendicular to the field, the potential energy of a magnetic dipole of moment m at angle theta to a uniform field B is
questions.a: -m B cos(theta)

questions.q: The torque on a magnetic needle in a uniform magnetic field is greatest when the angle between its magnetic moment and the field is ____ degrees (write a whole number).
Which statement about a magnetic dipole of moment m placed in a uniform magnetic field B is NOT correct?
questions.a: It experiences a net force in the direction of B
o: It experiences a net force in the direction of B
The torque on it tends to align m with B
Its potential energy is lowest when m is parallel to B
The torque on it vanishes when m is anti-parallel to B

questions.q: The orientation in which the magnetic moment is anti-parallel to the uniform field is called the most unstable position of a dipole because there
questions.a: the potential energy has its maximum value
o: the potential energy has its maximum value
the torque has its maximum value
the net force has its maximum value

questions.q: Why is the torque on a magnetic needle displaced from the direction of a uniform field called a restoring torque?
questions.a: Because it tends to turn the magnetic moment back towards the direction of B
o: Because it tends to turn the magnetic moment back towards the direction of B
Because it tends to increase the angle between m and B
Because it pushes the needle bodily along the field
Because it acts only when the needle is at rest

questions.q: A magnetised needle in a uniform magnetic field experiences a torque but no net force, yet an iron nail near a bar magnet experiences a net force as well. The reason is that
questions.a: the field of the bar magnet at the nail is non-uniform and induces a magnetic moment in the nail
o: the field of the bar magnet at the nail is non-uniform and induces a magnetic moment in the nail
the nail carries a net magnetic charge
a uniform field cannot act on a magnetised body at all
the nail is heavier than the needle

questions.q: An iron nail brought near the north pole of a bar magnet is attracted. Explain why the net force on the nail is attractive rather than zero.
questions.a: The bar magnet induces a magnetic moment in the nail, with the induced south pole nearer the magnet's north pole and the induced north pole farther away. Because the magnet's field is non-uniform (stronger nearer the pole), the attraction on the nearer induced south pole exceeds the repulsion on the farther induced north pole, giving a net attractive force.
s: Induced magnetic moment - unlike (south) pole induced nearer the magnet
Non-uniform field: attraction on the nearer pole exceeds repulsion on the farther pole

questions.q: A magnetic dipole of moment m in a uniform field B is turned from the position where m is parallel to B to the position where m is perpendicular to B. Its potential energy
questions.a: increases by mB

questions.q: A bar magnet of magnetic moment 0.50 J/T is placed with its axis at 30 degrees to a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. Use sin 30 degrees = 0.50 and cos 30 degrees = 0.87. What is the magnitude of the torque on it?

A bar magnet of magnetic moment 0.40 J/T lies with its magnetic moment parallel to a uniform field of 0.25 T. Taking the potential energy to be zero when the moment is perpendicular to the field, what is its potential energy?

A short bar magnet placed with its axis at 30 degrees to a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T experiences a torque of magnitude 4.0 x 10^-2 N m. Use sin 30 degrees = 0.50. The magnetic moment of the magnet, in J/T and as a decimal, is ____.

A bar magnet of magnetic moment 2.0 J/T lies aligned with the direction of a uniform magnetic field of 0.25 T. Find the work an external torque must do to turn the magnet so that its magnetic moment is (i) normal to the field and (ii) opposite to the field.
questions.a: Work done = change in potential energy = U_final - U_initial, with U = -m B cos(theta) and mB = 2.0 x 0.25 = 0.50 J. Initially theta = 0, so U = -0.50 J. (i) theta = 90 degrees: U = 0, so W = 0 - (-0.50) = 0.50 J. (ii) theta = 180 degrees: U = +0.50 J, so W = 0.50 - (-0.50) = 1.0 J.
s: W = U_final - U_initial with U = -m B cos(theta); mB = 0.50 J
(ii) W = 1.0 J

questions.q: A bar magnet of magnetic moment 1.5 J/T is in a uniform field of 0.20 T. What are the magnitudes of the torque on it when its moment is (i) normal to the field and (ii) opposite to the field?

A closely wound solenoid of 1000 turns and area of cross-section 2.0 x 10^-4 m^2 carries a current of 3.0 A and is suspended so that it can turn in a horizontal plane. A uniform horizontal magnetic field of 0.50 T is set up at 30 degrees to the axis of the solenoid. Use sin 30 degrees = 0.50. Find the magnetic moment of the solenoid, and the net force and the torque on it.
questions.a: Magnetic moment m = N I A = 1000 x 3.0 x 2.0 x 10^-4 = 0.60 A m^2, along the axis. The field is uniform, so the net force on the solenoid is zero. Torque = m B sin(theta) = 0.60 x 0.50 x 0.50 = 0.15 N m, in the sense that tends to align the axis (magnetic moment) with the field.

Net force = 0 because the field is uniform
Torque = m B sin(theta) = 0.15 N m, tending to align m with B

questions.q: Assertion (A): A magnetic needle held with its magnetic moment perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field is in equilibrium. Reason (R): With the choice of constant made in the chapter, the potential energy of the needle is zero when its magnetic moment is perpendicular to the field. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, R is true
o: A is false, R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false

questions.q: A small magnetised needle P is fixed at the origin with its magnetic moment along the +y direction. An identical needle Q is placed on the y-axis (the axis of P) at a large distance from P, with its magnetic moment along the -y direction. Q is free only to rotate about its own centre. Is Q in equilibrium, and if so is the equilibrium stable or unstable? Give the reason.
questions.a: On its axis the field of P is along P's magnetic moment, that is along +y. The moment of Q is along -y, anti-parallel to this field, so the torque on Q is zero and Q is in equilibrium. But with its moment anti-parallel to the field its potential energy is maximum, so the equilibrium is unstable.
s: Field of P on its axis is along +y; Q's moment is anti-parallel, so torque is zero (equilibrium)
Potential energy is maximum, so the equilibrium is unstable

questions.q: A small magnetised needle P is fixed at the origin with its magnetic moment along +y. An identical needle Q, of the same magnetic moment, is placed at the same large distance r from P in two ways: (i) on the y-axis with its moment along +y; (ii) on the x-axis with its moment along -y. Analyse whether each arrangement is a stable equilibrium and decide which has the lower potential energy.
questions.a: (i) On the axis of P the field is (mu0/4 pi)(2m/r^3) along +y. Q's moment is parallel to it, so the equilibrium is stable and U = -m B = -(mu0/4 pi)(2 m^2/r^3). (ii) On the equatorial line of P the field is (mu0/4 pi)(m/r^3) along -y, opposite to P's moment. Q's moment along -y is parallel to this field, so the equilibrium is again stable, with U = -(mu0/4 pi)(m^2/r^3). The axial field is twice the equatorial field, so arrangement (i) has the lower (more negative) potential energy.
s: (i) axial field along +y, Q parallel to it - stable
(ii) equatorial field along -y, Q parallel to it - stable
Axial field is twice as large, so (i) has the lower potential energy

questions.q: A student claims: 'The torque on a bar magnet is zero both when it is parallel and when it is anti-parallel to a uniform field, so no work is needed to turn it from one position to the other.' Evaluate the claim.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. The work done equals the change in potential energy, which is +mB - (-mB) = 2mB, not zero. The torque is zero only at the two end positions; at every angle in between a restoring torque m B sin(theta) acts and the external agent must work against it.
s: Judgement - claim is wrong; work = change in potential energy = 2mB
Reason - torque is non-zero at the intermediate angles

questions.q: A magnetic needle of known magnetic moment m is pivoted in a uniform magnetic field of unknown magnitude B. Design a method to find B from a torque measurement, stating the relation you would use.
questions.a: Hold the needle at a known angle theta to the field, most simply perpendicular to it (theta = 90 degrees), where the torque is largest. Measure the torque tau needed to hold the needle at rest in that position, for example with a calibrated spring or torsion arrangement. Then use tau = m B sin(theta), so B = tau/(m sin(theta)); for theta = 90 degrees, B = tau/m.
s: Set the needle at a known angle to the field (e.g. 90 degrees)
Measure the torque needed to hold it there
Use B = tau/(m sin(theta))

concepts.name: Gauss's law for magnetism
concepts.description: Magnetic flux through a closed surface, Gauss's law for magnetism, its contrast with Gauss's law of electrostatics, and its use in judging field-line diagrams.
concepts.idea: The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero, because magnetic field lines form closed loops and isolated magnetic poles do not exist.
concepts.rule: The magnetic flux through a small vector area element Delta S is Delta phi_B = B . Delta S; flux is a scalar measured in weber (1 Wb = 1 T m^2). Summing over all the area elements of a closed surface gives Gauss's law for magnetism: the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero, since as many field lines leave the surface as enter it. In electrostatics the flux of E through a closed surface is q/epsilon0, where q is the enclosed charge. The difference reflects the fact that isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) are not known to exist: there are no sources or sinks of B, and the simplest magnetic element is a dipole or a current loop. If monopoles existed, the right-hand side would be mu0 q_m, with q_m the magnetic charge enclosed. Consequences used to judge diagrams: magnetic field lines can never emanate from a point or a plate; they never cross; a closed loop of static magnetic field line must enclose a region across which a current passes, whereas electrostatic field lines never form closed loops; lines inside a toroid are closed loops confined within the windings; solenoid lines must curve out at the ends and close; lines between pole pieces must fringe at the ends; around either pole of a bar magnet the net flux is zero because lines also run inside the magnet. No element exerts a force or torque on itself through its own field, but one element of a current-carrying wire can act on another element. A system with zero net charge can still have a magnetic moment.
concepts.example: Field lines drawn as closed loops confined within the windings of a toroid are a correct magnetic picture: every loop encloses a region through which the current of the windings passes, and the net flux through any closed surface is still zero.

questions.q: Gauss's law for magnetism states that the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is
questions.a: zero
o: mu0 times the current enclosed by the surface
the enclosed electric charge divided by epsilon0
proportional to the area of the surface

questions.q: The weber, the unit of magnetic flux, is equal to
questions.a: 1 T m^2

questions.q: The magnetic flux through a small vector area element Delta S, where the field is B, is defined as
questions.a: the scalar product B . Delta S
o: the scalar product B . Delta S
the vector product B x Delta S
B divided by the magnitude of Delta S
mu0 times the scalar product B . Delta S

questions.q: Which of the following can NOT be a correct picture of static magnetic field lines?
questions.a: Lines radiating outward in all directions from a single point
o: Lines radiating outward in all directions from a single point
Closed loops encircling a long straight current-carrying wire
Closed loops confined within the windings of a toroid
Loops that run through the inside of a bar magnet and return outside it

questions.q: The difference between Gauss's law for magnetism and Gauss's law of electrostatics reflects the fact that
questions.a: isolated magnetic poles are not known to exist
o: isolated magnetic poles are not known to exist
magnetic fields are always weaker than electric fields
magnetic field lines can never pass through a closed surface
charges at rest produce no electric field

questions.q: Electrostatic field lines, unlike static magnetic field lines, can never
questions.a: form closed loops

questions.q: According to the chapter, the simplest magnetic element, out of which all magnetic phenomena can be built, is
questions.a: a dipole or a current loop
o: a dipole or a current loop

questions.q: A closed surface drawn around one end of an electric dipole has a net outward electric flux, but a closed surface drawn anywhere around a bar magnet has zero net magnetic flux. Explain the difference.
questions.a: The surface around the positive end of an electric dipole encloses a net charge, and electric field lines begin on it, so more lines leave than enter and the net flux is q/epsilon0. Magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops with no sources or sinks, because isolated magnetic poles do not exist, so every line that leaves a closed surface also enters it and the net magnetic flux is zero.
s: Electric case - surface encloses a net charge on which lines begin, so net flux is non-zero
Magnetic case - lines are closed loops (no monopoles), so lines leaving equal lines entering

questions.q: If magnetic monopoles existed, the right-hand side of Gauss's law for magnetism would, by analogy with electrostatics, become (q_m is the magnetic charge enclosed)
questions.a: mu0 q_m

questions.q: A closed surface is placed in a magnetic field. The total magnetic flux entering through one part of the surface is 3.0 x 10^-4 Wb. What is the total flux leaving through the rest of the surface?
A closed cubical surface completely encloses a bar magnet of magnetic moment 2.0 A m^2. The net magnetic flux through the surface of the cube, in weber and as a number, is ____.
A diagram shows field lines as straight lines radiating outward from a long straight wire, perpendicular to it. Explain why these cannot be magnetic field lines and say what they do represent.
questions.a: Magnetic field lines can never emanate from a wire or a point: a closed surface around the wire would then have a net outward flux, but the net flux of B through any closed surface must be zero. The lines shown are the electric field lines of a long positively charged wire. The correct magnetic field lines of a current-carrying straight wire are circles around the wire.
s: Net flux through a closed surface round the wire would be non-zero, violating Gauss's law for magnetism
They are electric field lines of a positively charged wire (magnetic lines circle the conductor)

questions.a: impossible, because a closed loop of static magnetic field line must enclose a region across which a current passes
o: impossible, because a closed loop of static magnetic field line must enclose a region across which a current passes
possible, because all magnetic field lines form closed loops
possible, provided the loop is a perfect circle
impossible, because magnetic field lines never form closed loops

questions.q: Outside a bar magnet the field lines spread out from the north-pole end. A student concludes that a closed surface enclosing only the north-pole end has a net outward magnetic flux, just like a closed surface enclosing a positively charged plate. Explain the error and contrast the two cases.
questions.a: Not all the field lines start at the north pole: the lines continue inside the magnet, and these interior lines enter the closed surface through the part of it that cuts the magnet. They exactly balance the lines leaving outside, so the net magnetic flux through the surface is zero, as Gauss's law for magnetism requires for any closed surface. For the positively charged plate the electric field lines really do begin on the enclosed charge, so the net electric flux is q/epsilon0 and is not zero.
s: Field lines also run inside the magnet and enter the surface there
So net magnetic flux through the surface is zero (Gauss's law for magnetism)
Charged plate - lines begin on the enclosed charge, net flux q/epsilon0 is non-zero

questions.q: Consider these statements. (I) Magnetic field lines between two flat pole pieces can be exactly straight right up to the edges of the pole pieces, with no fringing at all. (II) A system whose net electric charge is zero can still have a non-zero magnetic moment. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only II

questions.q: Does a bar magnet exert a torque on itself due to its own field? Does one element of a current-carrying wire exert a force on another element of the same wire? Answer both with a brief reason.
questions.a: No: there is no force or torque on an element due to the field produced by that element itself, so a magnet exerts no torque on itself. Yes: one element of a current-carrying wire does exert a force on a different element of the same wire, although for the special case of a straight wire this force is zero.
s: No self-torque - an element feels no force or torque from its own field
Yes - one element acts on another element of the same wire (zero for a straight wire)

questions.q: Compare Gauss's law of electrostatics with Gauss's law for magnetism under three heads: the statement of each law, the physical fact behind the difference, and what each implies about the field lines.
questions.a: Statement: the electric flux through a closed surface equals q/epsilon0, where q is the charge enclosed; the magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero. Physical fact: isolated electric charges exist, but isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) are not known to exist, so B has no sources or sinks and the simplest magnetic element is a dipole or current loop. Field lines: electric field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges (or go to infinity) and never form closed loops; magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops, so as many enter a closed surface as leave it.
s: Statements - electric flux = q/epsilon0; magnetic flux = 0
Reason - electric charges can be isolated, magnetic monopoles are not known to exist
Field lines - electric begin and end on charges; magnetic form closed loops

questions.q: A student says: 'Gauss's law for magnetism only tells us that something is zero, so it has no real content.' Evaluate this view.
questions.a: The view is mistaken. The zero expresses a physical fact: there are no sources or sinks of B, that is, isolated magnetic poles do not exist and the simplest magnetic element is a dipole or current loop. The law is also a working test: any diagram in which magnetic field lines emanate from a point, wire or plate can be rejected because it would give a non-zero flux through a closed surface.
s: Judgement - the law has content: it says monopoles do not exist / B has no sources or sinks
Use - lets us reject field-line pictures with net flux through a closed surface

questions.q: Compose your own example of a field-line pattern that is impossible for a magnetic field but possible for an electrostatic field. Describe the pattern in words, justify with Gauss's law why it cannot be magnetic, and name a charge arrangement that produces it.
questions.a: Example: lines that all leave an upper flat plate and all end on a parallel lower plate. A closed surface surrounding the upper plate has lines only leaving it, so the net flux through it is not zero; this is impossible for B, whose net flux through every closed surface is zero. The pattern is the electrostatic field between a positively charged upper plate and a negatively charged lower plate. (Lines radiating from a point, produced by a point positive charge, is an equally acceptable example.)
s: Pattern described - lines emanating from a plate or a point and not returning
Not magnetic - net flux through a closed surface round the source is non-zero
Charge arrangement named - e.g. oppositely charged plates or a point charge

concepts.name: Magnetisation, magnetic intensity, susceptibility and permeability
concepts.description: The definitions of magnetisation M and magnetic intensity H, the relation B = mu0(H + M), and the linked quantities susceptibility, relative permeability and permeability.
concepts.idea: The field in a material is split into a part H set by external currents and a part M contributed by the material, with M = chi H and B = mu0 (1 + chi) H = mu H.
concepts.rule: Magnetisation M of a sample is its net magnetic moment per unit volume, M = m_net/V, a vector measured in A/m. A long solenoid of n turns per unit length carrying current I has interior field B0 = mu0 n I. If its interior is filled with a material of non-zero magnetisation, the field becomes B = B0 + Bm, where the contribution of the core is Bm = mu0 M. The magnetic intensity is defined as H = B/mu0 - M, also measured in A/m, so B = mu0 (H + M). H represents the contribution of external factors such as the current in the solenoid (H = n I inside the solenoid), while M is due to the specific nature of the material. M depends on H through M = chi H, where chi is the dimensionless magnetic susceptibility: small and positive for paramagnetic materials and small and negative for diamagnetic ones (M and H then opposite). Hence B = mu0 (1 + chi) H = mu0 mu_r H = mu H, where mu_r = 1 + chi is the dimensionless relative magnetic permeability (the analog of the dielectric constant) and mu = mu0 mu_r is the magnetic permeability, with the same units as mu0. Only one of chi, mu_r and mu is independent. The magnetising current is the additional current that the windings would need, without the core, to give the same B as with the core.
concepts.example: A solenoid of 400 turns per metre carrying 1.5 A with a core of relative permeability 250 has H = 600 A/m, B = mu_r mu0 H = 250 x 4 pi x 10^-7 x 600 = about 0.19 T and M = 249 H, about 1.5 x 10^5 A/m.

the thermal motion of the atoms

Given one, the other two are determined, so only one is independent

questions.a: A is true, R is false
o: A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Material X has susceptibility +2 x 10^-5 and material Y has susceptibility -2 x 10^-5. Each is placed in the same magnetic intensity H. Compare the direction of the magnetisation and the size of B relative to mu0 H in the two materials.
questions.a: In X, M = chi H is along H (chi positive), so B = mu0 (1 + chi) H is slightly greater than mu0 H. In Y, M is opposite to H (chi negative), so B is slightly less than mu0 H. The change is tiny in both, about two parts in 10^5.

questions.q: A solenoid of n turns per metre carries a current of 2.0 A and has a core of relative permeability 500. The magnetising current I_M is the additional current that would have to be passed through the windings, with the core removed, to give the same field B as with the core. Working with exact relations (do not round B), find I_M.
questions.a: With the core: B = mu_r mu0 n I. Without the core but with the extra current: B = mu0 n (I + I_M). Equating, mu0 n (I + I_M) = mu_r mu0 n I, so I + I_M = mu_r I and I_M = (mu_r - 1) I = 499 x 2.0 = 998 A.

Without core B = mu0 n (I + I_M); equate the two

questions.q: A student says: 'B and H both describe the magnetic field in a material, so they are really the same quantity.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is not correct. H = B/mu0 - M accounts only for the external factors such as the current in the windings, while B = mu0 (H + M) also includes the contribution of the material through its magnetisation M. They even have different units: B is in tesla and H is in A/m. They are proportional (B = mu H) but not the same quantity.
s: Judgement - not the same; B includes the material's magnetisation, H only the external factors
Support - B = mu0 (H + M), or the different units T and A/m

questions.q: Starting from B = mu0 (H + M) and M = chi H, construct the chain of relations that leads to B = mu H, naming each new quantity you introduce.
questions.a: Substitute M = chi H: B = mu0 (H + chi H) = mu0 (1 + chi) H. Define the relative magnetic permeability mu_r = 1 + chi, a dimensionless quantity, so B = mu0 mu_r H. Define the magnetic permeability of the substance mu = mu0 mu_r = mu0 (1 + chi), which has the same units as mu0, so that B = mu H.
s: B = mu0 (1 + chi) H
mu_r = 1 + chi, relative magnetic permeability (dimensionless)
mu = mu0 mu_r, magnetic permeability, giving B = mu H

concepts.name: Diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic materials
concepts.description: Classifying materials by susceptibility and relative permeability, and the behaviour, atomic origin and examples of diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic substances.
concepts.idea: Materials are diamagnetic (chi negative), paramagnetic (chi small and positive) or ferromagnetic (chi large and positive), according to how their atomic magnetic moments respond to an applied field.
concepts.rule: Classification: diamagnetic, -1 <= chi < 0, 0 <= mu_r < 1, mu < mu0; paramagnetic, chi small and positive, mu_r slightly greater than 1, mu > mu0; ferromagnetic, chi much greater than 1, mu_r much greater than 1, mu much greater than mu0. Diamagnetic substances tend to move from the stronger to the weaker part of a field and are repelled by a magnet; field lines are expelled and the field inside is slightly reduced (about one part in 10^5). Their atoms have zero resultant magnetic moment, and an applied field induces a net moment opposite to the field. Examples: bismuth, copper, lead, silicon, nitrogen (at STP), water, sodium chloride. Diamagnetism is present in all substances but is usually masked by paramagnetism or ferromagnetism. Superconductors are perfect diamagnets (chi = -1, mu_r = 0): field lines are completely expelled, the Meissner effect. Paramagnetic substances are weakly magnetised and weakly attracted, moving from weak to strong field; their atoms have permanent dipole moments that random thermal motion keeps disordered, and a field partly aligns them, so the field inside is slightly enhanced. Examples: aluminium, sodium, calcium, oxygen (at STP), copper chloride. Their chi and mu_r depend on temperature; magnetisation rises with stronger field or lower temperature up to saturation, when all dipoles are aligned. Ferromagnetic substances are strongly magnetised and strongly attracted. Their atomic dipoles align spontaneously within domains (typically 1 mm, about 10^11 atoms); an external field orients the domains and makes favourably oriented ones grow. Hard ferromagnets (Alnico, lodestone) keep their magnetisation and form permanent magnets; soft ferromagnets (soft iron) lose it when the field is removed. Iron, cobalt, nickel and gadolinium are ferromagnetic, with mu_r above 1000. At a high enough temperature a ferromagnet becomes a paramagnet.
concepts.example: A material with mu_r = 0.99990 (chi = -1.0 x 10^-4) is diamagnetic; one with mu_r = 1.00050 is paramagnetic; iron, with mu_r above 1000, is ferromagnetic.

questions.q: In a non-uniform magnetic field, a diamagnetic substance tends to move
questions.a: from the stronger to the weaker part of the field

from the weaker to the stronger part of the field

questions.q: The atoms of a paramagnetic material have permanent magnetic dipole moments, yet the material shows no net magnetisation in the absence of a field. Why?
questions.a: Because ceaseless random thermal motion keeps the atomic dipoles pointing in random directions
o: Because ceaseless random thermal motion keeps the atomic dipoles pointing in random directions
Because the dipole moment of each atom is exactly zero
Because the dipoles are locked into domains that cancel in pairs
Because the atoms carry no moving charges

questions.q: When a bar of paramagnetic material is placed in an external magnetic field, the field lines
questions.a: get concentrated inside the bar, so the field inside is slightly enhanced
o: get concentrated inside the bar, so the field inside is slightly enhanced
are pushed out of the bar, so the field inside is slightly reduced
are completely expelled from the bar
pass through exactly as if the bar were absent

questions.q: Each domain of an unmagnetised piece of iron has a net magnetisation, yet the piece as a whole shows none. Explain this, and say what an external magnetic field does to the domains.
questions.a: The direction of magnetisation varies randomly from domain to domain, so the contributions cancel and there is no bulk magnetisation. When an external field is applied, the domains orient themselves along the field and the domains already oriented along the field grow in size, so the piece becomes strongly magnetised.
s: Magnetisation varies randomly from domain to domain, so no bulk magnetisation
External field - domains orient along it and favourably oriented domains grow

questions.q: For a superconductor, which behaves as a perfect diamagnet, the susceptibility chi and relative permeability mu_r are
questions.a: chi = -1 and mu_r = 0

questions.q: A material is found to have magnetic susceptibility -1.7 x 10^-5. The material is
questions.a: diamagnetic

questions.q: A small rod suspended by a thread near one pole of a strong magnet is pulled weakly towards the region of stronger field. The rod is most likely

questions.q: Three materials have relative permeabilities X: 0.99998, Y: 1.00002 and Z: 5000. Which classification is correct?
questions.a: X diamagnetic, Y paramagnetic, Z ferromagnetic
o: X diamagnetic, Y paramagnetic, Z ferromagnetic

questions.q: A strongly magnetised iron sample is heated to a high enough temperature. State what happens to its ferromagnetism and explain why.
questions.a: At a high enough temperature the ferromagnet becomes a paramagnet. The domain structure, in which atomic dipoles are aligned over macroscopic regions, disintegrates as the temperature rises, so the strong magnetisation disappears (gradually).
s: It becomes paramagnetic / loses its ferromagnetism
Because the domain structure disintegrates with temperature

questions.a: slightly reduced, by about one part in 10^5

questions.q: Three small rods A, B and C are hung in turn near one pole of a strong magnet, where the field is non-uniform. A is pulled strongly towards the pole, B is pulled weakly towards it and C is pushed weakly away. Classify each rod and, for each, state the sign and size of its susceptibility.
questions.a: A is ferromagnetic: it is strongly attracted, moving strongly from weak to strong field; chi is positive and large (much greater than 1). B is paramagnetic: it is weakly attracted towards the stronger field; chi is positive and small. C is diamagnetic: it moves from the stronger to the weaker part of the field, being weakly repelled; chi is negative and small.
s: A ferromagnetic - chi large and positive
B paramagnetic - chi small and positive
C diamagnetic - chi small and negative

questions.q: Consider these statements about magnetic materials. (I) Diamagnetism is present in all substances, but in most cases it is so weak that it is masked by effects such as paramagnetism or ferromagnetism. (II) A typical ferromagnetic domain is about 1 mm in size and contains about 10^11 atoms. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: Compare the atomic origin of diamagnetism with that of paramagnetism.
questions.a: In a diamagnetic substance the resultant magnetic moment of each atom is zero; an applied field induces a net magnetic moment opposite to the field, so the substance is repelled. In a paramagnetic substance each atom (or ion or molecule) has a permanent magnetic dipole moment; an applied field tends to align these moments along the field, so the substance is weakly magnetised in the direction of the field and attracted.
s: Diamagnetic - zero resultant atomic moment; field induces a moment opposite to it
Paramagnetic - permanent atomic moments that tend to align along the field

questions.q: Analyse why the magnetisation of a paramagnetic material increases when the applied field is increased or the temperature is lowered, what is meant by its saturation value, and why a ferromagnetic material is magnetised far more strongly in the same field.
questions.a: In a paramagnet the applied field tends to align the permanent atomic dipoles while random thermal motion disorders them; a stronger field or a lower temperature tips the balance towards alignment, so the magnetisation increases. Saturation is reached when all the dipoles are perfectly aligned with the field, after which the magnetisation cannot increase further. In a ferromagnet the atomic dipoles interact so that they align spontaneously within domains; the field only has to orient the domains and make favourable ones grow, so the material is strongly magnetised.
s: Field aligns dipoles, thermal motion disorders them - stronger field or lower temperature gives more alignment
Saturation - all dipoles perfectly aligned with the field
Ferromagnet - dipoles already aligned within domains by mutual interaction

questions.q: A student claims: 'Copper is non-magnetic, so a magnetic field has no effect on it at all.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is not strictly correct. Copper is diamagnetic: in a magnetic field it acquires a small magnetisation opposite to the field and is weakly repelled, moving from stronger to weaker field. The effect is very small (the field inside changes by about one part in 10^5), which is why it is hard to notice in everyday experience.
s: Judgement - not correct; copper is diamagnetic and is weakly repelled
The effect is very weak (about one part in 10^5), so it goes unnoticed

questions.q: You must choose a ferromagnetic material for (i) a compass needle and (ii) a core that should lose its magnetism as soon as the external field is switched off. Propose a suitable type of material for each, with an example, and justify your choices.
questions.a: (i) Compass needle: a hard ferromagnetic material, such as Alnico (or lodestone), because its magnetisation persists after the external field is removed, so it stays a permanent magnet. (ii) Core that must lose its magnetism: a soft ferromagnetic material, such as soft iron, because its magnetisation disappears when the external field is removed. The choice follows from whether the magnetisation of the material persists or not once the field is gone.
s: (i) hard ferromagnet, e.g. Alnico or lodestone - magnetisation persists
(ii) soft ferromagnet, e.g. soft iron - magnetisation disappears on removing the field
Justification based on retention versus loss of magnetisation
